results.title: How to Clear Lithium Battery Equipment Through Customs 5Best
results.content:
Sodium-ion is a genuine trap: the UN3551 and UN3552 entries apply only to sodium-ion with organic electrolyte. Sodium-ion batteries with aqueous alkaline electrolyte fall under a different entry entirely, UN2795 (Batteries, wet, filled with alkali), which is Class 8 corrosive, not Class 9. The chemistry and electrolyte must be confirmed before classification, not assumed. [...] Need help clearing lithium battery equipment through customs? ## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is UN38.3 required for sodium-ion batteries? [...] The UN number depends on the chemistry and configuration. Lithium-ion is UN3480 (alone) or UN3481 (packed with or contained in equipment). Lithium-metal is UN3090 or UN3091. For sodium-ion, the 67th edition of the IATA DGR introduced UN3551 (batteries shipped alone) and UN3552 (batteries packed with or contained in equipment) for cells and batteries with organic electrolyte.

results.title: U.S. CBP Revises Tariff Classification for Lithium Ion Cells ...
results.content:
The U.S. Customs & Border Protection (CBP) published a Notice that would revoke the Agency’s previous rulings on lithium ion cells in favor of classifying cells in the U.S. harmonized tariff schedule (HTS) applicable to batteries. Until 2018, the CBP’s tariff classification position on cells and batteries was of little practical importance because there was no difference in the duties applicable to imports under any of the applicable codes. However, the CBP’s stance took on heightened [...] took on heightened importance beginning in 2018, when the first Trump Administration imposed additional tariffs of 25% on Chinese lithium ion battery parts while imposing lower additional duties of 7.5% on Chinese lithium ion batteries. ## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the US tariff on lithium-ion batteries?

Lithium-ion batteries are classified under HTS 8507.60 with a base duty rate of 3.4%. Section 301 tariffs on Chinese-origin lithium-ion batteries add 25%, bringing the effective rate to 28.4% for Chinese imports.

## How do you find the US import duty for batteries? [...] Yes, EV battery cells and packs from China face Section 301 tariffs of 25% on top of the base 3.4% duty. This has accelerated battery production shifts to South Korea, Japan, and domestic US facilities.

### What HTS code is used for batteries?

Batteries fall under HTS 8507 (electric accumulators). Lithium-ion is 8507.60, lead-acid is 8507.10, nickel-metal hydride is 8507.50. Each has different base duty rates ranging from 2.7% to 3.4%.

Sodium-ion batteries have no lithium, cobalt, or nickel – making them entirely insulated from the tariff pressures affecting lithium-based chemistries. Industry analysis projects sodium-ion could capture 30 to 40 percent of the stationary storage market within five years. For OEM applications, sodium-ion is currently best suited for lower-energy applications in controlled temperature environments – industrial equipment, stationary backup power, urban delivery vehicles – rather than high-density [...] Sodium-ion batteries use sodium ions instead of lithium ions for charge transport, eliminating lithium, cobalt, and nickel from the chemistry entirely. This makes sodium-ion batteries maximally insulated from the current tariff environment – none of the heavily tariffed materials are in the supply chain. However, the global sodium-ion supply chain is still immature, with limited qualified manufacturers and no established large-scale cell supply outside of China. For OEM programs launching in [...] NiMH (Nickel Metal Hydride)

No lithium – fully insulated from lithium tariffs. Lower energy density. Still viable for specific medical device and industrial applications where lithium approval is difficult or where cycle life at low C-rates matters.

No lithium, cobalt, or nickel. Maximum tariff insulation. Immature supply chain. Best suited for stationary and low-energy applications. Significant OEM opportunity in 2028 and beyond when supply chains mature.

results.title: Navigating the Tariff Storm: Strategies for the U.S. Battery Industry Amidst Uncertainty
results.content: The United States has recently implemented substantial duties on imported goods, particularly targeting those from China, which holds a dominant position in the global battery supply chain. For instance, the tariff rate on Chinese EV lithium-ion batteries saw a sharp increase from 7.5% to 25% in 2024, and was set to reach a combined rate of 173% by April 2025 going forward, only to be put on pause by the same administration that created the executive order to institute them in the first place. [...] Exploring Alternative Chemistries: The reliance on mature chemistries like LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate), which are currently dominated by China, is encouraging exploration of alternative battery chemistries. Technologies like sodium-ion batteries, which have the potential to utilize domestically abundant materials, are being investigated as a long-term path to reduce reliance on foreign supply chains. For stationary energy storage, especially, sodium-ion battery systems offer a promising [...] Leveraging Duty Drawback Programs: For companies exporting finished products that incorporate imported, dutiable materials, the U.S. CBP offers a duty drawback program. This allows for a refund of duties paid on imported goods when those goods (or articles manufactured from them) are exported. Companies increasing non-China sourcing and manufacturing in the U.S. can support customers in utilizing this program for battery-related duties on exported equipment.
